passage: Masi Nandini handed Shreya a flat box in shiny paper on her birthday. Shreya tore it open: socks with tiny ducks. Her face fell. "I don't like this," she said, loudly. Masi Nandini's smile dipped and she looked down at her hands, hurt. Shreya's mother, Avni, knelt beside her and whispered, "Say thank you, and tell her it was thoughtful. You can tell me the rest later." Shreya swallowed and said, "Thank you, Masi." Masi Nandini said lightly, "Little ones do tell the truth, don't they?" and added gently that saying thanks matters. At home that night Shreya sniffled and told Mummy, "I wanted the toy dog." Avni hugged her. "You can feel sad. The socks are Masi's way of saying she loves you." The next week Shreya wore the duck socks to visit Masi and said, "My toes are warm," and Masi Nandini laughed.

qa.q: What was inside the box Shreya opened?
qa.a: It held socks with tiny ducks.

qa.q: How did Shreya's first reaction to the socks differ from how she handled it after her mother whispered, and how did each affect Masi Nandini?
qa.a: At first she said I don't like this loudly, which hurt Masi Nandini; after Avni's whisper she said thank you, and only at home did she tell her real feeling, that she wanted the toy dog.

qa.q: What was Masi Nandini feeling when Shreya said she did not like the socks?
qa.a: She felt hurt, since her smile dipped and she looked down at her hands, though she understood small children say what they feel.

qa.q: How could Avni keep helping Shreya with gifts she does not like?
qa.a: She could keep teaching her to say thank you first and listen to her real feelings at home, reminding her that the gift is someone's love.

grounding: A young child gets socks instead of a toy, says her dislike aloud, is guided to say thank you and later voices the truth in private while the giver feels hurt but understands.

passage: Sarika never broke a rule, and she said so, rolling her eyes when Manjula ran in the corridor. "You'll get in trouble. So silly." Manjula's shoulders dropped, and she stopped sitting next to Sarika. On Thursday Sarika's friend Dev kicked a ball through the library window during break. "Don't tell," he whispered. Sarika's heart raced, and she wanted to say it was the wind. Instead she said, "I won't lie, but I'll go with you to Ma'am Sangeeta." Dev shook his head. That night Sarika replayed the moment, and the heavy feeling sat in her chest like a stone: she had not helped Dev, and she had been unkind to Manjula. Next morning she told Dev, "Let's go now," and walked beside him into the staff room. Ma'am Sangeeta stayed calm, thanked them for telling her and said, "Let's work out how to fix the window. Dev will help the caretaker and write a note." Dev breathed out. Sarika then said sorry to Manjula and offered her the seat back. Manjula smiled. Sarika felt lighter, and she stopped telling herself she was better than anyone.

qa.q: What did Dev kick through the library window?
qa.a: Dev kicked a ball through the library window.

qa.q: How did Sarika's scorn for Manjula differ from her loyalty toward Dev?
qa.a: She rolled her eyes at Manjula for running and made her lonely, while with Dev she refused to lie but walked beside him to the teacher, showing that kindness and firmness can sit together.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling that night as she replayed the moment?
qa.a: She felt guilty, with a heavy feeling in her chest like a stone.

qa.q: What could Dev do next after the teacher's calm reply?
qa.a: He could help the caretaker and write the note as Ma'am Sangeeta said, and own up sooner if he breaks a rule again.

grounding: One child's contempt for a rule-breaker, loyalty to a friend who broke a rule, guilt that leads to sorry, and a teacher's calm response to honesty.

passage: Last month Seema had beaten Lakshmi's team and made a show of it, telling everyone, "Lakshmi runs like a snail." It felt sweet for a moment. Lakshmi stopped talking to her, and some classmates stopped clapping for Seema. Today, in the final, Seema scored the winning goal from a pass by Ravi. She felt wonderful, arms up, shouting. When the whistle blew she hugged Maria and thanked the whole team. Ravi was kicking the grass, quiet, and would not look up; he had wanted that chance. Seema said, "Your pass made the goal. I wouldn't have scored without it. Next corner is yours." Ravi shrugged, then almost smiled. Seema did not pretend she had not scored, and she kept her medal on. Then she walked over to Lakshmi, who had captained the losing side and stood alone with her water bottle. "Great game," Seema said. "Your save in the first half was brilliant. Next time you might beat us." Lakshmi's face eased. "Maybe," she said. "Good luck in the next round."

qa.q: Who passed to Seema for the winning goal?
qa.a: Ravi passed to Seema for the winning goal.

qa.q: How did Seema's behaviour after beating Lakshmi last month differ from her behaviour after the final?
qa.a: Last month she showed off and said Lakshmi runs like a snail, which cost her respect; after the final she thanked the team, credited Ravi's pass and spoke kindly to Lakshmi, keeping her medal on without gloating.

qa.q: What was Ravi feeling as he kicked the grass and would not look up?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a little envious, because he had wanted that chance.

qa.q: What could Seema do next time she wins?
qa.a: She could keep thanking her teammates, crediting their passes and being kind to the losers, remembering that she may lose next time. 🙂

grounding: A child who once gloated over a rival wins a final and shows pride with thanks, credit for a sulking teammate and kindness to the losing side.

passage: The caller said he was from Avni's bank and that her card would be blocked in ten minutes unless she read out the code that had just arrived. His voice was warm and hurried. Avni's heart raced, and she nearly read it out. Instead she said, "I'll call the number on the back of my card," and hung up. Later at work Pranav looked grey. A recruiter had asked him for an upfront fee for a job, and he had paid. He could not bring himself to tell a soul. Avni sat beside him and said, "Scammers count on shame. Let's report it now." They rang his bank and filed on the cyber portal within the hour. Pranav, furious, wanted to hunt the fraudster down; Avni said, "Put that into the complaint instead." He gathered screenshots and the transaction ID and posted a warning for his friends. That weekend her uncle Chaitanya phoned, shaky: he had sent money to a fake courier. Avni did not scold him or remind him of any warnings. She helped him stop the next payment and report it, and they agreed a habit: call her before paying anyone new.

qa.q: What did the caller say would happen in ten minutes?
qa.a: He said her card would be blocked.

qa.q: How did Avni's response to the caller differ from what happened to Pranav, and what did she then do for him?
qa.a: Avni nearly read out the code but hung up and planned to call the number on her card, while Pranav paid an upfront fee to a fake recruiter and hid it; Avni sat beside him and got him to report to his bank and the cyber portal within the hour.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he looked grey at work?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, too much to tell anyone that he had been scammed.

qa.q: What could Avni do next to help her uncle Chaitanya feel safe?
qa.a: She could keep supporting his safety habit of calling her before paying anyone new, and stay kind without blaming him.

grounding: Four moments around online scams: a friendly urgent caller, a friend's shame after losing money, his anger turned into a report and a relative's fresh loss met with compassion.

passage: Professor Himani had once told Raghav to leave a dull thesis topic and try soil sensors, and it changed his direction. He thanked her with a handwritten note. She had noticed how he hung on her words, and said, "I don't have every answer. Test my ideas and argue with me." Now a first-year, Meena, listened to Raghav's every sentence about the project. He told her honestly, "I don't know that part. Ask Professor Himani or read this paper," and passed on Himani's advice to try things herself first. Mohit, a senior in the lab, took Raghav's data for his own poster with no mention and asked him to stay late three weekends in a row. Raghav's face went hot. He said calmly, "I'd like my name on the poster, and I can't do weekends anymore." Mohit shrugged, so Raghav took it to Professor Himani, who set up a meeting with them both. In another course, project marks kept going to a professor's favourite. Raghav noted the rubric, compared the scores and wrote to the department head with the facts, and he kept working on his own project with the same care.

qa.q: What did Raghav switch to on Himani's advice?
qa.a: He switched to soil sensors.

qa.q: How did Himani's guidance differ from Mohit's treatment of Raghav?
qa.a: Himani changed his direction, admitted she did not have every answer and told him to test her ideas, while Mohit took Raghav's data for his own poster with no mention and asked him to stay three weekends.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he saw Mohit using his data?
qa.a: His face went hot, so he felt angry and treated unfairly.

qa.q: What could Raghav do next to protect his work and keep his own standards?
qa.a: He could keep using the proper channels with Himani and the department head, and keep passing on what he learns to first-years like Meena.

grounding: One student's mentor changes his direction, a professor's honesty about limits, a senior's unfair use of his work and a favouritism problem are handled with thanks, limits and facts.

passage: At dinner Papa said, "Our neighbour's boy already writes his whole name. Why can't you?" Mridul's ears went hot, and he pushed his plate away, stubborn. Then Mummy added, "Why can't you be more like your sister Arohi?" Mridul felt less loved and glared at Arohi, who had done nothing. Later, in a small voice, he said to Papa, "It makes me sad when you say that." Papa was quiet, then said, "I'm sorry. I liked how you tried the letter M today." At school a girl called Prisha ran the fastest in the race. Mridul watched, fired up and a bit envious, and asked, "Can you teach me to run like that?" Prisha showed him how to swing his arms. In art he looked at the neat colouring of the girl beside him and covered his own page with his arm. Rehana Ma'am crouched next to him. "See how much you've grown since September. Now most of your colours stay inside." Mridul smiled and slid his page back.

qa.q: What did Papa say the neighbour's boy could already write?
qa.a: He said the neighbour's boy could already write his whole name.

qa.q: How did Mridul's response to Papa's comparison differ from his response to Prisha's speed?
qa.a: With Papa's comparison he felt hurt and stubborn, pushing his plate away until he said it made him sad; with Prisha's speed he felt fired up and a bit envious and asked her to teach him.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when Mummy said he should be more like Arohi?
qa.a: He felt less loved and angry, so he glared at Arohi even though she had done nothing.

qa.q: What could Papa keep doing to help Mridul?
qa.a: He could keep praising Mridul's own progress, like trying the letter M, instead of comparing him with others.

grounding: A young child feels the hurt of comparison with a neighbour and a sister, the inspiration of a fast classmate and shame about neat colouring turned into pride in growth.
